questions.stem: Which tense is „Das Rathaus war schon 1990 renoviert worden“?
questions.explanation: „War“ (the imperfect of „sein“) plus a participle plus „worden“ makes the pluperfect passive: 'had been renovated'. The perfect passive would use „ist … worden“.

questions.stem: Which word completes „Die neue Brücke ___ nächstes Jahr eröffnet werden.“ ('will be opened')?
questions.explanation: The future passive is „werden“ as the future auxiliary, a participle, and the infinitive „werden“ at the end. „Würde“ would make it conditional ('would be opened') and „wurde“ past.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the passive of „Man baut hier ein neues Stadion“?
questions.explanation: The active sentence is in the present, so the passive needs present „wird“ plus the participle „gebaut“. „Wurde“ shifts it into the past, and „wird … bauen“ is the active future.

questions.stem: Compare „Die Geschäfte werden um acht geschlossen“ and „Die Geschäfte sind sonntags geschlossen“. What is the difference?
options: The first is written German; the second is only used in speech
The first describes the act of closing; the second describes a state
The first is in the present tense; the second is in the perfect tense
The first is an active sentence; the second is a passive sentence
questions.explanation: „Werden“ plus a participle is the action passive (someone closes the shops at eight). „Sein“ plus a participle is the state passive: the shops are in a closed state on Sundays. The perfect passive would need „worden“.

questions.stem: Which word completes „Das Bild wurde ___ einer jungen Künstlerin gemalt.“?
questions.explanation: The person who carries out a passive action is introduced by „von“ with the dative. „Mit“ names an instrument (mit einem Pinsel), not the person doing the action.

questions.stem: What does „Bei uns wird viel gelacht“ mean?
options: There is a lot of laughing at our place
We laugh at other people a lot when we are together
questions.explanation: This is an impersonal passive: the action itself is the focus and there is no subject. Being laughed at would be „Wir werden oft ausgelacht“, with „wir“ as the subject.

questions.stem: What does „Hier darf nicht geraucht werden“ mean?
questions.explanation: A modal plus a participle plus „werden“ is the passive infinitive with a modal: 'may not be smoked'. „Darf nicht“ is a prohibition, whereas 'need not' would be „muss nicht“ or „braucht nicht“.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I was told that the course is full'?
options: „Mir wurde gesagt, dass der Kurs voll ist.“
„Ich wurde gesagt, dass der Kurs voll ist.“
„Mich wurde gesagt, dass der Kurs voll ist.“
„Ich bin gesagt worden, dass der Kurs voll ist.“
questions.explanation: „Sagen“ takes a dative person (jemandem etwas sagen), and the dative stays dative in the passive, so it is „mir“. English makes 'I' the subject, but „ich wurde gefragt“ works only because „fragen“ takes the accusative.

questions.stem: Which words complete „Die Straße ___ wegen des Unfalls gesperrt ___.“ ('had to be closed')?
questions.explanation: A modal in the past plus a passive infinitive: „musste gesperrt werden“. „Worden“ belongs only in the perfect tenses of the passive, and it never follows a modal.

questions.stem: What does „Ich weiß, dass das Problem früher hätte gelöst werden müssen“ mean?
options: I know the problem could not be solved earlier
I know the problem should have been solved earlier
I know the problem had to be solved earlier
I know the problem will have to be solved soon
questions.explanation: „Hätte … müssen“ is the past subjunctive of a modal, so it describes something that should have happened and did not. 'Had to be solved' is the indicative „musste gelöst werden“, which states that it was necessary and implies it was done.

questions.stem: What does „Das lässt sich leicht erklären“ mean?
options: He explains it easily to himself
questions.explanation: „Sich lassen“ plus an infinitive is an alternative to the passive with „können“: „Das kann leicht erklärt werden“. It is common in formal writing and reads more naturally than a string of passives.

questions.stem: What does „Der Antrag ist bis Freitag einzureichen“ mean?
options: The application is being written until Friday
The application must be submitted by Friday
The application was submitted on Friday
The application can be collected on Friday
questions.explanation: „Sein“ plus „zu“ plus an infinitive expresses necessity in the passive, typical of official notices. „Einreichen“ is separable, so „zu“ goes inside it: „einzureichen“.

questions.stem: What is the Konjunktiv II of „kommen“ for „er“?
questions.explanation: Strong verbs form Konjunktiv II from the imperfect stem plus an umlaut and „-e“: „kam“ becomes „käme“. „Kam“ is the plain imperfect, and „kämme“ belongs to „kämmen“, to comb.

questions.stem: What is the Konjunktiv II of „wissen“ for „ich“?
questions.explanation: „Wissen“ takes an umlaut on its imperfect stem: „ich wusste“ becomes „ich wüsste“, as in „Wenn ich das nur wüsste!“. Without the umlaut it is simply the past.

questions.stem: Which is the politest way to ask a stranger for a moment of their time?
questions.explanation: Konjunktiv II „hätten“ softens the request, and „vielleicht“ softens it further. „Hast du“ is informal, and the imperative „Nehmen Sie sich Zeit!“ is an instruction, not a request.

questions.stem: What does „Wenn ich das gewusst hätte, wäre ich früher gekommen“ mean?
options: If I know that, I will come earlier
If I had known that, I would have come earlier
If I knew that, I would come earlier
When I found that out, I came along a little earlier
questions.explanation: „Hätte gewusst“ and „wäre gekommen“ are past subjunctive forms, so both clauses are about a past that did not happen. The present subjunctive 'if I knew' would be „wenn ich das wüsste“.

questions.stem: Which pair completes „Wenn wir den Bus nicht verpasst ___, ___ wir pünktlich gewesen.“?
questions.explanation: Each clause keeps its own auxiliary: „verpassen“ takes „haben“, so „verpasst hätten“, and „sein“ takes „sein“, so „wären … gewesen“. Using one auxiliary for both is the usual slip.

questions.stem: In „Hätte ich mehr Geld, würde ich eine Weltreise machen“, what does the first clause mean?
questions.explanation: When „wenn“ is left out, the verb moves to the front of the clause. „Hätte ich mehr Geld“ is therefore a condition, not a question, and the comma and main clause confirm it.

questions.stem: Which completes „Sie sagte, dass sie ___.“ ('that she should have stayed at home')?
questions.explanation: With a double infinitive in a subordinate clause, the auxiliary does not go last: it comes in front of the two infinitives. The modal stays an infinitive, „sollen“, rather than becoming „gesollt“.

questions.stem: Which completes „Er tut so, als ob er nichts davon ___.“ ('as if he knew nothing about it')?
questions.explanation: „Als ob“ introduces something presented as untrue, so it takes Konjunktiv II, and as a subordinating conjunction it sends the verb to the end. „Weißt“ is the „du“ form and does not agree with „er“.

questions.stem: What does „Wenn ich doch nur mehr Zeit hätte!“ express?
options: A wish: if only I had more time!
A plan: when I have more time
A fact: I had more time back then
A demand: give me more time!
questions.explanation: „Wenn … doch nur“ with Konjunktiv II expresses a wish that is unlikely to come true. A plan would use the indicative, as in „wenn ich mehr Zeit habe“.

questions.stem: What does „Es wäre besser gewesen, wenn du früher angefangen hättest“ mean?
options: It would be better if you started earlier
It would have been better if you had started earlier
It will be better if you start earlier
It was better when you started earlier
questions.explanation: „Wäre … gewesen“ and „hättest … angefangen“ are both past Konjunktiv II, so the sentence is a criticism of what did not happen. 'Would be better if you started' is present: „wäre besser, wenn du anfangen würdest“.

questions.stem: What does „Der neue Lehrer soll sehr streng sein“ mean?
options: The new teacher has to be very strict
The new teacher wants to be very strict
The new teacher ought not to be strict
The new teacher is said to be very strict
questions.explanation: Besides 'should', „sollen“ can report what others say: 'is supposed to be' in the sense of hearsay. Obligation would be „muss“, and „soll“ here passes on a rumour.

questions.stem: What does „Er will den Text allein übersetzt haben“ mean?
options: He wanted to have the text translated for him
He will have translated the text on his own
He claims to have translated the text on his own
He wants to translate the text on his own
questions.explanation: „Wollen“ with a past infinitive („übersetzt haben“) means to claim, and it hints that the speaker doubts it. „Will“ is not a future marker in German; the future uses „werden“.

questions.stem: What does „Sie muss krank sein – sie ist heute nicht gekommen“ express?
options: A report that she was ill but came to school anyway
A conclusion that she is probably ill, drawn from her absence
A rule that she has to stay at home on any day that she is ill
A wish that she were ill so that she could stay at home
questions.explanation: „Müssen“ can express a confident inference: 'she must be ill'. The second clause gives the evidence, which is what marks this as a conclusion rather than an obligation.

questions.stem: Which completes „Er war enttäuscht, weil er nicht ___.“ ('because he had not been able to come')?
questions.explanation: The pluperfect of a modal with another verb uses a double infinitive, „kommen können“. In a subordinate clause the auxiliary „hatte“ goes in front of the double infinitive, not after it.

questions.stem: What does „Sie wird wohl im Stau stehen“ mean?
options: She wants to stand in the traffic
She was stuck in traffic for a while
She is probably stuck in traffic
She will be stuck in traffic tomorrow
questions.explanation: „Werden“ with „wohl“ expresses a guess about the present, not a future event. The particle „wohl“ (probably) is the signal that this is supposition.

questions.stem: Which completes „Er erzählte, dass er sein Auto ___.“ ('had had his car washed')?
questions.explanation: „Lassen“ with an infinitive forms its perfect tenses with a double infinitive, „waschen lassen“, not „gelassen“. In the „dass“ clause the auxiliary „hatte“ goes in front of the two infinitives.

questions.stem: What does „Ich kann mich nicht daran gewöhnen, so früh aufzustehen“ mean?
options: I can't remember getting up so early
I can't be bothered getting up so early
I can't believe I got up so early
I can't get used to getting up so early
questions.explanation: „Sich gewöhnen an“ is to get used to. „Daran“ points forward to the „zu“ infinitive clause, a pattern German uses whenever a prepositional verb is followed by a clause.

questions.stem: Which preposition completes „Alles hängt ___ dem Wetter ab.“?
questions.explanation: „Abhängen von“ is to depend on, always with the dative. English 'on' tempts learners towards „an“ or „auf“, but the verb fixes the preposition.

questions.stem: Which preposition completes „Er nimmt ___ einem Austauschprogramm teil.“?
questions.explanation: „Teilnehmen an“ plus the dative is to take part in. „In“ is the English-led guess; the dative „einem“ fits „an“ here because the verb requires it.

questions.stem: Which preposition completes „Ich erinnere mich gern ___ meine Zeit in Wien.“?
questions.explanation: „Sich erinnern an“ takes the accusative, which is why it is „meine Zeit“. Translating 'remember about' or 'remember of' word for word leads to the wrong preposition.

questions.stem: Which preposition completes „Nach drei Jahren im Ausland sehnt sie sich ___ ihrer Familie.“?
questions.explanation: „Sich sehnen nach“ (to long for) takes the dative, which is why „ihrer Familie“ follows. „Für“ follows English 'long for' but is not the German pattern.

questions.stem: What does „Du fehlst mir sehr“ mean?
options: You are very wrong about me
I am missing a lot of things
questions.explanation: „Fehlen“ takes the dative of the person who feels the absence: literally 'you are missing to me'. The roles are the reverse of English, which is why 'you miss me' is the common mistake.

questions.stem: Which word completes „Gestern ___ ich zufällig meiner alten Lehrerin begegnet.“?
questions.explanation: „Begegnen“ (to meet by chance) takes the dative and forms its perfect with „sein“. Both features break the English pattern, which is why „habe“ is so tempting.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Er widerspricht ___ Chef nie.“?
questions.explanation: „Widersprechen“ (to contradict) is one of the verbs that take the dative, so the masculine possessive becomes „seinem“. „Seinen“ would treat the boss as a direct object.

questions.stem: What does „In diesem Artikel geht es um die Zukunft der Arbeit“ mean?
options: This article is going to change the future of work
This article is about the future of work
This article goes on to the future of work
This article is written for future workers
questions.explanation: „Es geht um“ is the impersonal expression for what something is about. It is very common in text analysis, alongside „es handelt sich um“.

questions.stem: What does „Es lohnt sich, früh zu buchen“ mean?
options: It is easy to book early
It is necessary to book early
It is cheap to book early
questions.explanation: „Sich lohnen“ is to be worthwhile, and the impersonal „es“ points forward to the „zu“ infinitive. Cheap would be „günstig“; the sentence is about the benefit, not the price.

questions.stem: Why is it „übersetzt“, not „setzt … über“, in „Sie übersetzt den Brief ins Englische“?
options: Über- is always inseparable, whatever the verb means
The verb is in a subordinate clause, so it stays joined
Über- only separates from its verb in the perfect tense
Meaning 'translate', über- is an inseparable prefix
questions.explanation: Some prefixes are separable in one meaning and inseparable in another. „Übersetzen“ meaning to ferry across is separable („Der Fährmann setzt uns über“), but meaning to translate it never separates.

questions.stem: What does „Ich stelle mir das Leben in Berlin spannend vor“ mean?
options: I introduce myself to exciting life in Berlin
I present my exciting life in Berlin
I put my life in Berlin before others
I imagine life in Berlin to be exciting
questions.explanation: „Sich (dative) etwas vorstellen“ is to imagine something, while „sich (accusative) vorstellen“ is to introduce oneself. The dative „mir“ is the clue to the meaning.

questions.stem: Which word completes „___ Sie bitte pünktlich!“?
questions.explanation: The „Sie“ imperative of „sein“ is irregular: „Seien Sie …!“. „Seid“ is the „ihr“ form („Seid leise!“), and „Sind Sie pünktlich?“ is a question.

questions.stem: Which completes „Nachdem wir das Museum ___, gingen wir essen.“?
questions.explanation: „Nachdem“ marks the earlier of two past events, so it takes the pluperfect when the main clause is in the imperfect. „Hätten“ would turn a fact into a hypothetical.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Ich ___, du wärst schon weg.“ (denken)?
questions.explanation: „Denken“ is a mixed verb: it changes its stem like a strong verb but takes weak endings, giving „dachte“. „Bringen“ (brachte) and „kennen“ (kannte) follow the same pattern.
